title: BCI Classification
text: typical BCI classification workflow involves: 1. Preprocessing (filtering, artifact removal) 2. Feature extraction (CSP, bandpower, Riemannian geometry) 3. Classification (LDA, SVM cross-validation) 4. Performance evaluation (accuracy, kappa, information transfer rate)

title: BCI Classification
text: Create simulated BCI data motor imagery trials (left vs. right hand):
code: library(PhysioEEG) library(SummarizedExperiment) library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # Generate 80 trials: 40 left hand, 40 right hand # make_eeg_bci() creates n_trials PER class, so n_trials = 40 yields 80 total # 16 channels, 250 Hz sampling rate, 4-second trials eeg <- make_eeg_bci(   n_trials = 40,   n_channels = 16,   sr = 250,   trial_sec = 4 )  # Trial condition labels ("left"/"right") are stored in metadata condition <- metadata(eeg)$labels  # Examine data structure eeg dim(assay(eeg, "raw"))  # 1000 timepoints x 16 channels x 80 trials  # Check trial labels table(condition)  # Should show balanced left/right classes

title: BCI Classification
text: Motor imagery produces ERD movement imagination ERS task completion. eegMotorImagery() function computes power changes motor-related frequency bands. Visualize ERD/ERS patterns:
code: # Compute ERD/ERS in mu and beta bands eeg <- eegMotorImagery(   eeg,   bands = list(     mu = c(8, 12),     beta = c(13, 30)   ),   assay_name = "raw" )  # ERD/ERS results stored in metadata as an n_trials x (n_channels * n_bands) # matrix with column names "<channel>_<band>" (e.g. "C3_mu") erd_results <- metadata(eeg)$erd_ers  # Examine mu-band power changes (one column per channel) mu_cols <- grep("_mu$", colnames(erd_results)) mu_power <- erd_results[, mu_cols, drop = FALSE] head(mu_power)  # Laterality index LI = (R - L) / (|R| + |L|) from C4 (right) vs C3 (left). # Positive values indicate right-hemisphere dominance (left hand imagery), # negative values indicate left-hemisphere dominance (right hand imagery). lat <- eegLateralization(   eeg,   left_ch = "C3",   right_ch = "C4",   band = c(8, 12),   method = "power" ) laterality <- lat$per_trial   # per-trial LI (n_trials x 1) lat$summary                   # biomarker summary (mean LI with CI) # Plot per-channel mu-band ERD/ERS for left vs. right conditions library(ggplot2)  # Channel labels for the mu-band columns ch_names <- sub("_mu$", "", colnames(mu_power))  # Average mu-band power change per channel for each condition mu_left <- colMeans(mu_power[condition == "left", , drop = FALSE]) mu_right <- colMeans(mu_power[condition == "right", , drop = FALSE])  df_plot <- data.frame(   channel = factor(rep(ch_names, 2), levels = ch_names),   power = c(mu_left, mu_right),   condition = rep(c("Left", "Right"), each = length(ch_names)) )  ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = channel, y = power, fill = condition)) +   geom_col(position = "dodge") +   geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +   labs(     title = "Motor Imagery ERD/ERS (Mu Band)",     x = "Channel",     y = "Power Change (%)",     fill = "Condition"   ) +   theme_minimal() +   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

title: BCI Classification
text: CSP powerful technique extracting spatial filters maximize variance differences two classes. finds projections one class high variance low variance. Understanding CSP components:
code: # Apply bandpass filter to isolate the mu+beta band. # eegFilter() operates on continuous (2D) data, so band-pass each epoch's # channels (8-30 Hz, zero-phase Butterworth) into a new "filtered" assay. sr <- samplingRate(eeg) bf <- signal::butter(4, c(8, 30) / (sr / 2), type = "pass") raw3d <- assay(eeg, "raw") assay(eeg, "filtered") <- array(   apply(raw3d, c(2, 3), function(sig) signal::filtfilt(bf, sig)),   dim = dim(raw3d) )  # Extract CSP features # n_filters = 3 selects the 3 top + 3 bottom eigenvectors = 6 components eeg <- eegCSP(   eeg,   labels = condition,   n_filters = 3,   assay_name = "filtered" )  # CSP spatial filters stored in metadata as (n_components x n_channels); # transpose to view as channels x components csp_filters <- t(metadata(eeg)$csp$filters) dim(csp_filters)  # 16 channels x 6 components  # Projected data (log-variance features for classification) csp_features <- metadata(eeg)$csp_features dim(csp_features)  # 80 trials x 6 features # First components maximize variance for class 1 (left hand) # Last components maximize variance for class 2 (right hand)  # Visualize first CSP filter (most discriminative for left) filter_1 <- csp_filters[, 1] names(filter_1) <- colData(eeg)$label  # Create topographic visualization data topo_data <- data.frame(   channel = names(filter_1),   weight = filter_1 )  print(topo_data)  # Examine CSP feature distributions boxplot(   csp_features[, 1] ~ condition,   main = "CSP Component 1 (Left-specific)",   xlab = "Condition",   ylab = "Log Variance" )  boxplot(   csp_features[, 6] ~ condition,   main = "CSP Component 6 (Right-specific)",   xlab = "Condition",   ylab = "Log Variance" )

title: BCI Classification
text: eegBCIfeatures() function provides multiple feature extraction methods can combined robust classification. Bandpower-specific feature extraction: Riemannian geometry features:
code: # eegBCIfeatures() extracts one method per call and returns a matrix. # Collect the three feature families into a named list. features_all <- list(   bandpower  = eegBCIfeatures(eeg, method = "bandpower",  labels = condition,                               assay_name = "filtered"),   csp        = eegBCIfeatures(eeg, method = "csp",        labels = condition,                               assay_name = "filtered"),   riemannian = eegBCIfeatures(eeg, method = "riemannian", labels = condition,                               assay_name = "filtered") )  # Each list element is a feature matrix names(features_all)  # Bandpower features: power in specified frequency bands per channel bp_features <- features_all$bandpower dim(bp_features)  # 80 trials x (16 channels * n_bands)  # CSP features: log-variance of CSP-projected signals csp_features <- features_all$csp dim(csp_features)  # 80 trials x 6 components  # Riemannian features: tangent space projection of covariance matrices riem_features <- features_all$riemannian dim(riem_features)  # 80 trials x n_tangent_features # Extract power in the default mu/beta frequency bands features_bp <- eegBCIfeatures(   eeg,   method = "bandpower",   labels = condition,   assay_name = "raw" )  # Bandpower features are log band power per channel and band # (default bands: mu 8-13 Hz, beta 13-30 Hz)  # Normalize features (z-score per feature dimension) features_norm <- scale(features_bp)  # Examine feature importance via correlation with labels label_numeric <- ifelse(condition == "left", 0, 1) correlations <- cor(features_norm, label_numeric) head(sort(abs(correlations), decreasing = TRUE)) # Riemannian approach treats covariance matrices as points # on a manifold and projects to tangent space  features_riem <- eegBCIfeatures(   eeg,   method = "riemannian",   labels = condition,   assay_name = "filtered" )  # These features often outperform traditional methods # for BCI classification due to better handling of # non-Euclidean structure of covariance matrices  riem_data <- features_riem dim(riem_data)

title: BCI Classification
text: frequency-tagged visual stimuli, SSVEP analysis identifies target frequency EEG spectrum. Multi-frequency SSVEP (multi-class BCI):
code: # Detect SSVEP across candidate flicker frequencies using CCA. # Each candidate uses 3 harmonics in its reference signals. ssvep_results <- eegSSVEP(   eeg,   frequencies = c(12, 15, 20),   n_harmonics = 3,   assay_name = "raw" )  # Results: one row per candidate frequency with CCA correlation and SNR ssvep_results  # SNR at each candidate frequency (named by frequency) snr_values <- ssvep_results$snr names(snr_values) <- ssvep_results$frequency  # High SNR indicates a strong SSVEP response mean(snr_values) sd(snr_values)  # Binary detection: SSVEP present vs. absent (threshold at SNR = 3) ssvep_detected <- snr_values > 3 table(ssvep_detected) # In a multi-class SSVEP BCI, test several candidate target frequencies at once target_freqs <- c(7, 9, 11, 13)  # 4-class BCI  ssvep_all <- eegSSVEP(eeg, frequencies = target_freqs, n_harmonics = 2,                       assay_name = "raw")  # The candidate frequency with the highest SNR is the detected class predicted_freq <- ssvep_all$frequency[which.max(ssvep_all$snr)] predicted_freq

title: BCI Classification
text: eegBCIclassify() function performs classification cross-validation estimate generalization performance. Compare multiple classifiers: Feature comparison classification:
code: # eegBCIclassify() returns a per-trial data.frame of predictions # (columns: trial, predicted_class, confidence, true_class). Derive # accuracy, Cohen's kappa, and the confusion matrix from those predictions. bci_metrics <- function(res) {   lv <- sort(unique(c(res$true_class, res$predicted_class)))   cm <- table(     true = factor(res$true_class, levels = lv),     predicted = factor(res$predicted_class, levels = lv)   )   acc <- sum(diag(cm)) / sum(cm)   pe <- sum(rowSums(cm) * colSums(cm)) / sum(cm)^2   kappa <- if (pe < 1) (acc - pe) / (1 - pe) else NA_real_   list(accuracy = acc, kappa = kappa, confusion_matrix = cm) }  # Classify using CSP features and LDA # 5-fold cross-validation for robust performance estimation results_lda <- eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = csp_features,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 5 )  # Extract performance metrics m_lda <- bci_metrics(results_lda) accuracy_lda <- m_lda$accuracy kappa_lda <- m_lda$kappa confusion_lda <- m_lda$confusion_matrix  cat(sprintf("LDA Accuracy: %.2f%%\n", accuracy_lda * 100)) cat(sprintf("Cohen's Kappa: %.3f\n", kappa_lda)) print(confusion_lda) # LDA: Linear Discriminant Analysis (assumes Gaussian distributions) results_lda <- eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = csp_features,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 10 )  # Shrinkage LDA: regularized covariance estimate, robust for high-dimensional # feature spaces with limited trials results_slda <- eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = csp_features,   labels = condition,   method = "shrinkage_lda",   cv_folds = 10 )  # Compare performance m_lda <- bci_metrics(results_lda) m_slda <- bci_metrics(results_slda) comparison <- data.frame(   Method = c("LDA", "Shrinkage-LDA"),   Accuracy = c(m_lda$accuracy, m_slda$accuracy),   Kappa = c(m_lda$kappa, m_slda$kappa) )  print(comparison) # Classify using different feature sets # 1. CSP features acc_csp <- bci_metrics(eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = features_all$csp,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 5 ))$accuracy  # 2. Bandpower features acc_bp <- bci_metrics(eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = features_all$bandpower,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 5 ))$accuracy  # 3. Riemannian features acc_riem <- bci_metrics(eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = features_all$riemannian,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 5 ))$accuracy  # Compare feature sets feature_comparison <- data.frame(   Features = c("CSP", "Bandpower", "Riemannian"),   Accuracy = c(acc_csp, acc_bp, acc_riem) )  print(feature_comparison)

title: BCI Classification
text: ITR measures communication speed BCI bits per minute. depends accuracy, number classes, selection time.
code:
# ITR formula for binary classification: # ITR = (log2(N) + P*log2(P) + (1-P)*log2((1-P)/(N-1))) * (60/T) # where N = number of classes, P = accuracy, T = trial duration (sec)  calculate_itr <- function(accuracy, n_classes, trial_duration) {   if (accuracy <= 1/n_classes) return(0)  # Below chance    P <- accuracy   N <- n_classes    # Bits per trial   bits_per_trial <- log2(N) + P * log2(P) +                     (1 - P) * log2((1 - P) / (N - 1))    # Bits per minute   itr <- bits_per_trial * (60 / trial_duration)   return(itr) }  # For our 2-class BCI with 4-second trials itr <- calculate_itr(   accuracy = overall_acc,   n_classes = 2,   trial_duration = 4 )  cat(sprintf("Information Transfer Rate: %.2f bits/min
", itr))  # Compare different scenarios scenarios <- expand.grid(   accuracy = seq(0.6, 0.95, by = 0.05),   trial_duration = c(3, 4, 5) )  scenarios$itr <- mapply(   calculate_itr,   accuracy = scenarios$accuracy,   trial_duration = scenarios$trial_duration,   MoreArgs = list(n_classes = 2) )  # Find optimal configuration best <- scenarios[which.max(scenarios$itr), ] cat(sprintf("
Optimal configuration:

", best$accuracy * 100)) cat(sprintf("  Trial Duration: %.1f s
", best$trial_duration)) cat(sprintf("  ITR: %.2f bits/min
", best$itr))

title: BCI Classification
text: Proper cross-validation critical reliable performance estimation.
code: # 5-fold CV: Standard for small datasets (n < 100) cv5 <- eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = csp_features,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 5 )  # 10-fold CV: More reliable estimate, higher computational cost cv10 <- eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = csp_features,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = 10 )  # Leave-one-out CV: Maximum variance reduction (n = n_trials) # Only for small datasets due to computational cost cv_loo <- eegBCIclassify(   eeg,   features = csp_features,   labels = condition,   method = "lda",   cv_folds = nrow(csp_features)  # 80 folds = leave-one-out )  cv_comparison <- data.frame(   Method = c("5-Fold", "10-Fold", "Leave-One-Out"),   Accuracy = c(bci_metrics(cv5)$accuracy, bci_metrics(cv10)$accuracy,                bci_metrics(cv_loo)$accuracy),   Kappa = c(bci_metrics(cv5)$kappa, bci_metrics(cv10)$kappa,             bci_metrics(cv_loo)$kappa) )  print(cv_comparison)

Understanding interactions fundamental cognitive neuroscience, revealing distributed neural networks coordinate perception, cognition, action. Key Concepts: Functional connectivity: Statistical dependencies signals, regardless directionality (e.g., coherence, PLV, wPLI) Effective connectivity: Directed influence one region another (e.g., Granger causality) Volume conduction problem: Instantaneous spatial spread electrical activity tissue creates spurious connectivity doesn’t reflect true neural coupling PhysioEEG provides methods ranging basic coherence advanced phase-based metrics mitigate volume conduction artifacts.

Formula: Cxy(f)=|Pxy(f)|2Pxx(f)Pyy(f)C_{xy}(f) = \frac{|P_{xy}(f)|^2}{P_{xx}(f)P_{yy}(f)} PxyP_{xy} cross-spectral density PxxP_{xx}, PyyP_{yy} auto-spectral densities.

title: Connectivity Analysis
text: Interpretation: MSC > 0.5 alpha band O1-O2 indicates strong bilateral synchronization visual cortex rhythms. However, MSC sensitive volume conduction—high coherence may reflect passive spread rather true neural coupling.
code: # Compute coherence between occipital channels (O1-O2) in alpha band (8-12 Hz) # Expected to show strong coupling due to bilateral alpha rhythm coh_alpha <- eegCoherence(   eeg,   method = "coherence",  # magnitude-squared coherence   band = c(8, 12),   window_sec = 2,  # 2-second windows for spectral estimation   assay_name = "raw" )  # Result contains coherence values averaged over the frequency range print(coh_alpha)  # Compute broadband coherence for theta through gamma coh_broad <- eegCoherence(   eeg,   method = "coherence",  # magnitude-squared coherence   band = c(4, 40),   window_sec = 4,  # Longer window for lower frequencies   assay_name = "raw" )

Lower values expected reflect genuine neural interactions.
code: # Compute imaginary coherence to reduce volume conduction artifacts icoh_alpha <- eegCoherence(   eeg,   method = "imaginary",   band = c(8, 12),   window_sec = 2,   assay_name = "raw" )  # Compare with MSC to identify spurious connectivity # Large difference suggests volume conduction contamination

title: Connectivity Analysis
text: PLV measures phase consistency two signals across trials, independent amplitude fluctuations. makes PLV robust non-stationarities signal amplitude. Formula: PLV=|1N∑n=1NeiΔϕn|PLV = \left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N e^{\Delta\phi_n}\right| Δϕn\Delta\phi_n phase difference channels trial nn. Interpretation: PLV = 0: Random phase relationship across trials PLV = 1: Perfect phase alignment across trials PLV > 0.3: Generally considered moderate phase locking PLV > 0.5: Strong phase locking, indicates robust neural coordination PLV particularly useful event-related designs phase consistency changes experimental conditions. However, PLV can still affected volume conduction since zero-lag phase relationships can occur artifactually.
code: # Compute PLV in theta band (4-8 Hz) for frontal-central connectivity # Theta coupling reflects working memory and cognitive control processes plv_theta <- eegPLV(   eeg,   band = c(4, 8),   assay_name = "raw" )  # PLV in alpha band for posterior connectivity plv_alpha <- eegPLV(   eeg,   band = c(8, 12),   assay_name = "raw" )  # PLV in beta band (13-30 Hz) for motor coordination # Expected higher C3-C4 coupling during motor planning plv_beta <- eegPLV(   eeg,   band = c(13, 30),   assay_name = "raw" )

title: Connectivity Analysis
text: weighted phase lag index (Vinck et al., 2011) addresses volume conduction problem focusing non-zero phase lags, eliminating instantaneous correlations. Key advantage: wPLI insensitive volume conduction maintaining statistical power better imaginary coherence. use wPLI: High-density EEG nearby electrodes Source localization unavailable need robust connectivity estimates free zero-lag artifacts Comparing connectivity across different montages subjects Trade-: wPLI may lower sensitivity PLV, higher specificity genuine neural coupling.
code: # Compute wPLI in alpha band # More conservative estimate of true neural coupling wpli_alpha <- eegWPLI(   eeg,   band = c(8, 12),   assay_name = "raw" )  # wPLI across multiple frequency bands for comparison wpli_theta <- eegWPLI(eeg, band = c(4, 8)) wpli_beta <- eegWPLI(eeg, band = c(13, 30)) wpli_gamma <- eegWPLI(eeg, band = c(30, 50))  # Compare PLV vs wPLI to assess volume conduction impact # Large PLV but small wPLI suggests spurious connectivity

title: Connectivity Analysis
text: Spectral Granger causality quantifies directed (causal) influence frequency domain. tests whether past values signal X improve prediction signal Y beyond Y’s history. Interpretation: GCX→Y(f)GC_{X\Y}(f) represents reduction prediction error Y incorporating X’s history, frequency ff. Important caveats: Directionality ≠ anatomical causation: Granger causality reflects predictive relationships, necessarily anatomical connections Stationarity assumption: Time series must stationary; apply short epochs detrended data Common input problem: Shared inputs can create spurious Granger causality Model order: Critical parameter; use AIC/BIC selection physiologically motivated values Frequency-specific interpretation: High theta GC (4-8 Hz): Top-cognitive control High alpha GC (8-12 Hz): Attentional modulation High beta GC (13-30 Hz): Motor preparation sensorimotor feedback High gamma GC (30-80 Hz): Local processing feedforward sensory flow
code: # Compute Granger causality from frontal to parietal regions # Tests top-down attentional control hypothesis gc_frontal_parietal <- eegGrangerCausality(   eeg,   order = 10,          # Model order (typically 10-20 for EEG)   band = c(4, 40),   assay_name = "raw" )  # Model order selection is critical # Too low: Underfitting, missing dynamics # Too high: Overfitting, spurious causality  # Rule of thumb: order ≈ 2 × (sampling_rate / lowest_frequency_of_interest) # For 250 Hz and 4 Hz: order ≈ 2 × (250/4) = 125 samples, but use 10-20 for stability  # Compute bidirectional causality to assess feedback loops gc_parietal_frontal <- eegGrangerCausality(   eeg,   order = 10,   band = c(4, 40),   assay_name = "raw" )

code: # Proportional thresholding: Keep top 20% of connections threshold_prop <- quantile(conn_matrix_alpha[upper.tri(conn_matrix_alpha)], 0.80)  # Absolute thresholding: Keep connections above physiological significance threshold_abs <- 0.3  # For wPLI, values > 0.3 often indicate robust coupling  # Statistical thresholding: Compare against surrogate data distribution # (requires permutation testing, not shown here)  # Apply threshold to matrix conn_matrix_thresh <- conn_matrix_alpha conn_matrix_thresh[conn_matrix_thresh < threshold_prop] <- 0

title: Sleep EEG Analysis
text: Sleep complex physiological state characterized distinct stages, unique electroencephalographic (EEG) signatures. American Academy Sleep Medicine (AASM) defines five sleep stages: wakefulness (W), three non-REM stages (N1, N2, N3), rapid eye movement sleep (REM). Accurate sleep staging critical diagnosing sleep disorders, assessing sleep quality, understanding neurological health. Traditional sleep scoring time-intensive manual process performed trained polysomnographic technologists. vignette demonstrates PhysioEEG provides automated tools : Automatic sleep staging based AASM criteria using spectral features Detection sleep-specific waveforms: spindles, K-complexes, slow waves Quantification sleep architecture: total sleep time, efficiency, stage distribution Visualization: hypnograms clinical interpretation tools can accelerate research workflows, provide preliminary automated scoring clinical review, enable large-scale sleep studies.

Real sleep EEG also include EOG (eye movements) EMG (muscle tone) comprehensive staging.

code: # Flag 30-second epochs whose peak amplitude exceeds +/-150 uV as artifacts reref <- assay(eeg_filt, "reref") epoch_len <- 30 * samplingRate(eeg_filt) n_epochs <- nrow(reref) %/% epoch_len artifact_epochs <- Filter(function(e) {   seg <- reref[((e - 1) * epoch_len + 1):(e * epoch_len), , drop = FALSE]   max(abs(seg)) > 150 }, seq_len(n_epochs)) artifact_epochs <- unlist(artifact_epochs)  # Mark artifact epochs for exclusion from analysis metadata(eeg_filt)$artifact_epochs <- artifact_epochs

title: Sleep EEG Analysis
text: Wake (W): Low delta, high alpha (8-12 Hz) beta (>13 Hz) eyes open N1: Theta activity (4-7 Hz) dominates, alpha dropout N2: Sleep spindles (11-16 Hz bursts) K-complexes N3: High delta power (0.5-2 Hz), slow wave sleep (SWS) REM: Mixed frequency, low amplitude, theta sawtooth waves

title: Sleep EEG Analysis
text: Slow wave activity exhibits characteristic temporal dynamics:
code: # Full-night SWA dynamics (an exponential decline across sleep cycles) require # a complete overnight recording. Here we summarise slow-wave amplitude over # time by binning slow-wave events into successive segments of the recording. if (nrow(slow_waves) > 0) {   sw_time_min <- slow_waves$start_sample / samplingRate(eeg_filt) / 60   n_bins <- 5   bin <- cut(sw_time_min, breaks = n_bins, labels = FALSE)   swa_by_bin <- tapply(abs(slow_waves$negative_peak), bin, mean)    plot(seq_along(swa_by_bin), swa_by_bin,        type = "b", pch = 19,        xlab = "Recording segment", ylab = "Mean slow-wave amplitude (uV)",        main = "Slow Wave Amplitude Across the Recording") }

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: Time-frequency analysis essential understanding oscillatory brain activity changes time response stimuli cognitive tasks. Unlike classical ERP analysis focuses time-domain averages, time-frequency methods reveal dynamic spectral changes specific frequency bands (delta, theta, alpha, beta, gamma) often masked traditional averaging. Common neuroscience applications include: Event-Related Spectral Perturbation (ERSP): Power changes relative baseline specific frequency bands, revealing induced oscillatory activity may time-locked Intertrial Coherence (ITC): Phase consistency across trials, capturing evoked oscillatory responses Theta-gamma coupling: Investigating cross-frequency interactions memory encoding Mu/beta suppression: Motor imagery action observation studies Alpha desynchronization: Attentional modulation visual processing PhysioEEG provides three complementary time-frequency decomposition methods, distinct advantages depending research question, signal characteristics, required time-frequency resolution.

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
code: library(PhysioEEG) library(SummarizedExperiment)  # The single-signal transforms (Morlet, STFT, multitaper) operate on 2D # continuous data (time x channels); ERSP and ITC operate on 3D epoched data # (time x channels x trials) and compute the wavelet internally.  # 2D continuous data (19-channel 10-20 layout, 4 s at 500 Hz) eeg <- make_eeg(n_channels = 19, n_time = 2000, sr = 500)  # 3D epoched ERP data (40 trials of 1 s) for ERSP and ITC eeg_epochs <- make_eeg_erp(   n_channels = 19,   n_epochs = 40,   sr = 500,   epoch_sec = 1.0 )  # Inspect dimensions dim(assay(eeg, "raw"))         # timepoints x channels (continuous) dim(assay(eeg_epochs, "raw"))  # timepoints x channels x trials (epoched) samplingRate(eeg)              # 500 Hz

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: Morlet wavelet transform provides excellent time-frequency resolution trade-control via number cycles parameter. convolves signal complex Morlet wavelets specified frequencies, yielding power phase information. Parameter selection: Frequencies: Define frequency range based research question. general cognitive studies, 4-40 Hz captures theta low gamma. detailed alpha analysis, use finer spacing (e.g., 8-13 Hz 0.5 Hz steps). n_cycles: Controls time vs frequency resolution trade-. Lower values (3-5 cycles) provide better temporal precision broader frequency resolution; higher values (7-12 cycles) provide sharper frequency resolution smear events time. common compromise use frequency-dependent cycles: n_cycles = f / 3 (e.g., 4 Hz → 1.3 cycles, 40 Hz → 13 cycles). use Morlet wavelets: Default choice EEG time-frequency analysis Excellent event-related designs temporal precision matters Ideal need consistent time-frequency resolution across spectrum Preferred cross-frequency coupling analysis
code: # Detailed alpha-band analysis with higher frequency resolution eeg <- eegMorletWavelet(   eeg,   frequencies = seq(8, 13, by = 0.5),  # Fine-grained alpha range   n_cycles = 7,                         # More cycles for sharper frequency precision   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "alpha_power" )  # Broad-band Morlet transform (theta-gamma). eegMorletWavelet() uses a fixed # (scalar) number of cycles across frequencies. Stored under the default name # "wavelet_power", this is the product visualized in the spectrogram section. eeg <- eegMorletWavelet(   eeg,   frequencies = seq(4, 40, by = 2),    # 4-40 Hz in 2 Hz steps   n_cycles = 5,                         # good time-frequency compromise   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "wavelet_power" )  # Output (stored in metadata): timepoints x frequencies x channels dim(metadata(eeg)$wavelet_power)

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: STFT divides signal short overlapping windows computes FFT segment. provides uniform time-frequency resolution across frequencies, determined window size. Window size trade-offs: Window size: Larger windows (e.g., 1000 ms) provide better frequency resolution poor temporal precision. Smaller windows (e.g., 100 ms) capture rapid changes coarse frequency resolution. 200-500 ms window typical cognitive EEG. Overlap: Higher overlap (75-90%) provides smoother time-frequency representations increases computation. 50% overlap reasonable default. Window type: Hanning window reduces spectral leakage standard choice. Hamming window slightly better frequency resolution leakage. use STFT: uniform time-frequency resolution desired Continuous EEG resting-state data computational speed priority (faster wavelets many frequencies) need direct control time-frequency resolution physical units
code: # Standard STFT with 250 ms windows (good balance for cognitive EEG) eeg <- eegSTFT(   eeg,   window_sec = 0.25,      # 250 ms window   overlap = 0.75,         # 75% overlap for smooth representation   window_type = "hanning",   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "stft_power" )  # Output (stored in metadata): timepoints x frequencies x channels dim(metadata(eeg)$stft_power)  # For high temporal precision (e.g., rapid stimulus changes) eeg <- eegSTFT(   eeg,   window_sec = 0.1,       # 100 ms windows   overlap = 0.50,         # 50% overlap   window_type = "hanning",   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "stft_fast" )  # For high frequency resolution (e.g., resting-state narrow-band analysis) eeg <- eegSTFT(   eeg,   window_sec = 1.0,       # 1000 ms windows   overlap = 0.90,         # High overlap to maintain some temporal detail   window_type = "hamming",   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "stft_fine" )

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: Thomson multitaper method uses multiple orthogonal tapers (windowing functions) reduce variance spectral estimates maintaining good frequency resolution. provides robust spectral estimates, especially stationary quasi-stationary signals. Parameter selection: Bandwidth: Determines frequency smoothing number available tapers. Bandwidth 2-4 Hz typical EEG. Higher bandwidth provides tapers (lower variance) coarser frequency resolution. n_tapers: Number tapers use. tapers reduce variance increase smoothing. Typically set floor(2 * bandwidth * T - 1) T time window duration seconds. use multitaper: Resting-state continuous EEG quasi-stationary spectral content need robust spectral estimates minimal variance Narrow-band oscillation detection (e.g., individual alpha frequency) signal--noise ratio low Spectral analysis relatively long, stable epochs
code: # Multitaper analysis with 3 Hz bandwidth # Good for reducing noise in oscillatory power estimates eeg <- eegMultitaper(   eeg,   bandwidth = 3,          # 3 Hz smoothing bandwidth   n_tapers = 5,           # Use 5 Slepian tapers   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "multitaper_power" )  # Output (stored in metadata): timepoints x frequencies x channels dim(metadata(eeg)$multitaper_power)  # For high-frequency resolution (narrow-band analysis) eeg <- eegMultitaper(   eeg,   bandwidth = 1.5,        # Narrow bandwidth for fine frequency resolution   n_tapers = 3,   assay_name = "raw",   output_assay = "multitaper_narrow" )

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: ERSP quantifies time-frequency power changes relative baseline period, typically pre-stimulus. reveals event-related synchronization (ERS, power increase) desynchronization (ERD, power decrease), capturing induced oscillatory activity may strictly phase-locked stimulus. Baseline normalization methods: Decibel (dB): 10 * log10(power / baseline) - symmetric, interpretable percent change log scale Percent change: 100 * (power - baseline) / baseline - intuitive asymmetric Z-score: (power - mean_baseline) / sd_baseline - accounts variance, good statistics Interpreting ERSP: Positive values (ERS): Power increase relative baseline. Example: frontal theta increase memory encoding, gamma increase sensory processing. Negative values (ERD): Power decrease relative baseline. Example: central mu/beta suppression motor preparation, occipital alpha decrease visual attention. Time course: ERSP reveals spectral changes occur, distinguishing early sensory late cognitive processes. Spatial distribution: Topographic patterns indicate functional networks (e.g., frontal theta vs posterior alpha).
code: # eegERSP() takes the 3D epoched data and computes the Morlet wavelet and # baseline normalization internally. The baseline window is given in samples. freqs <- seq(4, 40, by = 2) eeg_epochs <- eegERSP(   eeg_epochs,   baseline = c(1, 50),   # baseline = first 50 samples (100 ms) of each epoch   frequencies = freqs,   n_cycles = 5,   assay_name = "raw" )  # ERSP stored in metadata (already averaged across trials) ersp_data <- metadata(eeg_epochs)$ersp_data dim(ersp_data)  # timepoints x frequencies x channels  # Extract single-channel ERSP for visualization pz_idx <- match("Pz", colData(eeg_epochs)$label) pz_ersp <- ersp_data[, , pz_idx] dim(pz_ersp)  # timepoints x frequencies

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: ITC measures phase consistency across trials time-frequency point, ranging 0 (random phase) 1 (perfect phase alignment). Unlike ERSP captures power changes, ITC specifically identifies phase-locked (evoked) oscillatory activity. Key concepts: ITC = 1: trials identical phase time-frequency point (perfect evoked response) ITC = 0: Random phase across trials (purely induced activity) ITC vs ERP: High ITC low frequencies corresponds traditional ERP components. However, ITC can also detect phase-locked higher-frequency oscillations invisible averaged ERP. Interpreting ITC: High ITC + high ERSP: Evoked power increase (phase-locked power increase) High ITC + low ERSP: Phase-locked activity without net power change (phase reset) Low ITC + high ERSP: Induced power increase without phase-locking (e.g., stimulus-triggered temporally jittered oscillations) Low-frequency ITC peaks: Correspond traditional ERP components (N1, P3, etc.) High-frequency ITC: May indicate early sensory-evoked gamma beta responses
code: # eegITC() computes the complex Morlet transform per trial internally and # measures phase consistency across trials from the 3D epoched data. eeg_epochs <- eegITC(   eeg_epochs,   frequencies = freqs,   n_cycles = 5,   assay_name = "raw" )  # ITC stored in metadata itc_data <- metadata(eeg_epochs)$itc_data dim(itc_data)  # timepoints x frequencies x channels  # Extract channel-specific ITC (Cz is a central fronto-central lead) cz_idx <- match("Cz", colData(eeg_epochs)$label) cz_itc <- itc_data[, , cz_idx] dim(cz_itc)  # timepoints x frequencies  # High ITC at low frequencies captures ERP phase-locking. # Theta-band (4-8 Hz) ITC time course: theta_cols <- which(freqs >= 4 & freqs <= 8) theta_itc <- rowMeans(cz_itc[, theta_cols, drop = FALSE]) plot(theta_itc, type = "l", xlab = "Time (samples)", ylab = "ITC")

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: Time-frequency heatmaps (spectrograms) standard visualization ERSP, ITC, raw power. PhysioEEG provides customizable spectrogram plotting sensible defaults. Visualization tips: ERSP: Use diverging colormaps (RdBu, RdYlBu) center zero distinguish ERS ERD ITC: Use sequential colormaps (viridis, magma, plasma) since values range 0 1 Raw power: Apply log scaling compress dynamic range make oscillations visible Frequency range: Narrow ranges (e.g., 8-13 Hz alpha) reveal fine structure; broad ranges (4-80 Hz) show multi-band dynamics Time range: Include pre-stimulus baseline contextualize post-stimulus changes
code: # Plot the Morlet power spectrogram for channel Pz eegPlotSpectrogram(   eeg,   channel = "Pz",   freq_range = c(4, 40),      # Focus on theta-gamma range   time_range = NULL,          # full time range (time axis is in seconds)   log_power = TRUE,           # convert power to dB scale   palette = "viridis",   assay_name = "wavelet_power" )  # Plot the spectrogram for a central lead (Cz) eegPlotSpectrogram(   eeg,   channel = "Cz",   freq_range = c(4, 30),   time_range = NULL,   log_power = TRUE,   palette = "viridis",   assay_name = "wavelet_power" )  # Zoom into the alpha band for an occipital channel eegPlotSpectrogram(   eeg,   channel = "O1",   freq_range = c(8, 13),      # Alpha band detail   time_range = NULL,   log_power = TRUE,           # Convert to dB scale   palette = "magma",   assay_name = "wavelet_power" )

title: Time-Frequency Analysis
text: Choosing right time-frequency method depends data characteristics, research question, computational resources. Decision tree: Epoched event-related data precise timing requirements: Use Morlet wavelets frequency-dependent n_cycles optimal time-frequency resolution matching signal characteristics. Continuous resting-state EEG: Use STFT speed multitaper robust spectral estimates low variance. Narrow-band oscillation detection (e.g., individual alpha frequency): Use multitaper low bandwidth superior frequency resolution. Broad frequency range varying dynamics: Use Morlet wavelets frequency-dependent parameters (low n_cycles low frequencies, high n_cycles high frequencies). Low signal--noise ratio: Use multitaper reduce spectral variance, average multiple Morlet wavelet trials. Computational constraints: Use STFT, faster wavelets analyzing many frequencies. Frequency resolution comparison: Wavelet: Resolution = f / n_cycles. Example: 10 Hz 5 cycles → 2 Hz resolution. STFT: Resolution = sampling_rate / window_size. Example: 500 Hz 250-sample window → 2 Hz resolution. Multitaper: Resolution ≈ bandwidth. Example: 3 Hz bandwidth → ~3 Hz resolution. Time resolution comparison: Wavelet: Resolution = n_cycles / f. Example: 10 Hz 5 cycles → 0.5 s resolution. STFT: Resolution = window_size / sampling_rate. Example: 250 samples 500 Hz → 0.5 s resolution. Multitaper: Resolution depends window size taper properties, generally moderate.

what: PhysioEEG: EEG Analysis Functions for PhysioExperiment Objects — PhysioEEG-package
title: PhysioEEG: EEG Analysis Functions for PhysioExperiment Objects — PhysioEEG-package
text: Provides comprehensive electroencephalography (EEG) analysis functions PhysioExperiment objects. Includes preprocessing (filtering, re-referencing, bad channel detection, interpolation, epoching, artifact rejection), independent component analysis (FastICA, Infomax, JADE) automatic artifact detection, event-related potential (ERP) component detection measurement (N100, P300, N400, P600, MMN), source localization (eLORETA, sLORETA, LCMV beamformer), EEG microstate analysis (K-means, AAHC), sleep staging (AASM criteria, spindle/K-complex/slow-wave detection), brain-computer interface features (CSP, SSVEP, motor imagery), clinical EEG analysis (spike detection, QEEG, asymmetry indices), time-frequency analysis (Morlet wavelet, STFT, multitaper, ERSP, ITC), connectivity analysis (coherence, PLV, wPLI, Granger causality), visualization (signal traces, ERP waveforms, topographic maps, spectrograms, connectivity plots, hypnograms, source maps), simulated data generators testing demonstration.

title: PhysioEEG 0.7.2
text: eegSourceEstimate(method = "dspm") adds dSPM (dynamic statistical parametric mapping; Dale et al. 2000): minimum-norm estimate noise-normalized source’s projected noise sensitivity (sqrt(diag(K K')) identity noise covariance). Verified MNE scaled per source time-invariant factor. eegDipoleFit() adds equivalent-current-dipole (ECD) fitting — focal complement distributed inverses. localizes single dipole best explains scalp topography (grid search inside head sphere refined Nelder-Mead; dipole moment closed-form least-squares fit position), using forward physics eegForwardModel(). Verified recover planted dipole’s position (< 0.02 head radii), orientation, > 99.9% goodness fit. Fits peak global-field-power sample default, chosen sample / window.

title: PhysioEEG 0.7.1
text: eegSurfaceLaplacian() adds surface Laplacian / current source density (CSD) Perrin et al. (1989) — spherical-spline scalp Laplacian (Kayser & Tenke 2006). CSD reference-free spatial high-pass, deblurring volume conduction channel reflects radial current beneath . Verified defining properties: invariance reference constant (spline constant term absorbs ) spatial-high-pass behaviour (focal topographies emphasized smooth ones ~8x). Reuses .legendre_poly recurrence standard 10-10/10-20 position tables; needs electrode positions (colData pos_x/pos_y/pos_z, else matched standard montage label).

title: PhysioEEG 0.7.0
text: Three research-grade method families missing EEG stack. eegComplexity() adds nonlinear / complexity family (previously absent ecosystem-wide EEG): per-channel sample & approximate entropy (Richman–Moorman, Pincus), permutation entropy (Bandt–Pompe), multiscale entropy (Costa), Lempel–Ziv complexity, Higuchi & Katz fractal dimension, detrended fluctuation analysis (alpha), Hurst (R/S), Hjorth parameters, spectral entropy. numeric cores validated known values (white noise Higuchi FD → 2, Brownian → 1.5; white-noise DFA/Hurst → 0.5). Entropy measures O(N^2) cap long channels via max_samples. eegAperiodic() adds aperiodic / 1-f spectral parameterization (specparam / FOOOF; Donoghue 2020): per-channel aperiodic exponent / offset / knee plus separated oscillatory peaks, ready topomap qEEG biomarker. Delegates fit PhysioAnalysis::specparam(). eegPAC() eegComodulogram() add phase-amplitude / cross-frequency coupling (Tort modulation index, Canolty mean-vector-length, Ozkurt, PLV), within channel across two channels, plus comodulogram grid. Delegate estimators PhysioCrossModal::phaseAmplitudeCoupling() / comodulogram(). reuse existing specparam PAC engines (new PhysioAnalysis Suggests; PhysioCrossModal already suggested) rather reimplementing , add genuinely new complexity module natively. existing behaviour changed.
